chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father and Ali ibn Muhammad, altogether from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Suleiman ibn Dawud, from Hafs ibn Ghiyas, who said:

One of my brothers wrote to me to ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about certain matters from the Sunnah. So I asked him, or wrote to him with them. Among what I asked him was: 'Inform me about the army when it battles in the land of war, acquires booty, and then another army joins them before they exit to the House of Peace (Dar al-Salam), and they did not encounter an enemy until they all exited to the House of Peace. Would they share in the booty?' He said: 'Yes'.

And about a raiding party that was in a ship, and the owner of the horse did not ride his horse. How is the booty distributed among them?' He said: 'For the horseman two shares, and for the foot soldier one share.'

I said: 'And if they did not ride and did not fight upon their horses?' He said: 'What do you think if they were in an army, and the foot soldiers were sent forward, fought, and acquired booty, how would it be distributed among them? Would I not have made two shares for the horseman and one share for the foot soldier, even though they acquired the booty without the horsemen?'
ai.seo_question: How is war booty distributed when armies join mid-campaign or when cavalry does not ride?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies two key principles of ghanimah distribution: first, that subsequent armies joining before the return to Dar al-Salam share equally in the spoils, and second, that the distinction between cavalry (two shares) and infantry (one share) is based on their designated role rather than actual combat performance or mount usage. This reflects the Shia scholarly understanding of the Prophetic precedent where status and readiness determined entitlement, ensuring fairness even when logistical realities (like riding vs. fighting on foot) varied among the troops.
